source.title: Dynamic Adaptive Threshold based Learning for Noisy Annotations Robust Facial Expression Recognition
source.authors: Darshan Gera; Naveen Siva Kumar Badveeti; Bobbili Veerendra Raj Kumar; S. Balasubramanian

record.file_problem: Full paper text supplied; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results on training with synthetic label corruption and explicitly describes a standard ResNet-18 cross-entropy baseline overfitting on noisy samples. This is relevant evidence about fitting corrupted labels, but does not test the claim’s completely random-label, chance-test-error, or unchanged-hyperparameter conditions; its proposed method changes the training procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper tests 10%, 20%, and 30% synthetic label noise, not completely random labels. Table 1 compares test accuracy across methods, and the text describes train/test curves for a baseline and DNFER under 30% noise. It does not report training error on random labels or test error at chance. Other discussion of Zhang et al. and Arpit et al. is cited prior work, not this study’s result. Figure 2’s curves have no extracted numeric values.
record.test_reason: The standard cross-entropy baseline provides a new-setting test of V4's test-performance component: accuracy decreases monotonically across 10%, 20% and 30% random label corruption on three FER datasets. Perfect training fit and degradation toward chance are not established. The mitigation method itself does not test the claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that dynamic class-specific selection for supervised learning, combined with consistency learning on all samples, mitigates noisy-annotation overfitting and performs effectively on synthetic and real noisy FER datasets.
record.recipe_differences: DNFER uses ResNet-18 with a dynamic class-specific sample-selection threshold, a warm-up phase, supervised loss on selected samples, and consistency loss on augmented views; the paper does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The text reports different performance by dataset and synthetic noise fraction, and says DNFER’s component-only variants fail as noise increases from 10–30% on RAFDB and FERPlus. Warm-up length and loss weight α are selected by ablation; precise figure values are not stated.
record.problems: The relevant train/test trajectories are provided as plots without numerical values in the supplied text. The synthetic-noise sweep reaches only 30%, and the reported table measures test accuracy rather than training error or fit to completely random labels.
record.rows_left_out: The component ablations on RAFDB and FERPlus across 0–30% noise (Figures 5 and 6), α sensitivity (Figure 7), and warm-up sensitivity (Figure 8) are described without recoverable numeric values. They do not establish the specific V4 outcomes of perfect training fit or test error approaching chance, so no separate rows were extracted. Results for DNFER and other methods in Table 1 are not rows because they do not measure the standard network behavior named in the claim.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, zero or near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged architecture/hyperparameters relative to true-label training.
Time needed to fit true versus random labels and convergence-time changes across corruption fractions.
Perfect training fit across corruption fractions; behavior beyond 30% through completely random labels; approach to chance; direct separation of signal learning from noise memorization.
Whether weight decay, dropout or augmentation prevent random-label fitting, and generalization after removing explicit regularization.
Separate learning trajectories for clean and corrupted examples or true versus random labels. The explicit clean-first statement cites prior work.

record.verdict_notes: Partial coverage of V4 is not evidence against its untested parts. R1–R9 states describe the observed degradation component collectively, not verification of the complete conjunction in V4. The implementation uses a face-recognition-pretrained ResNet-18 and Adam; the baseline supplies relevant evidence despite the paper's primary focus on mitigation.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test error, or unchanged architecture and training-hyperparameter comparison.
No comparison of training time to fit true versus random labels, nor a convergence-time sweep over corrupted-label fractions.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper evaluates 0–30% noise rather than noise rising to 100%, and does not report perfect training fit across those rates or a steadily rising test error toward chance. Figure 5 and Figure 6 provide component comparisons, but the supplied text gives no recoverable numeric values.
No test of weight decay, dropout, or whether removing regularization preserves generalization on true labels.
The paper describes a standard noisy-label learning pattern as prior work, but does not test whether its own networks learn true-label patterns before memorizing noise.

rows.subject: Baseline model (all samples, cross-entropy)
rows.operation_detail: Compared training and test accuracy during training under 30% synthetic label noise on RAFDB; the text reports training accuracy saturates and test accuracy rises initially then drops as training progresses.
rows.measure: Training and test accuracy over training
rows.baseline: DNFER training and test accuracy curves
rows.value: Training accuracy saturates; test accuracy initially increases, then drops as training progresses.
rows.note: Authors state the pattern for the baseline across RAFDB, FERPlus, and AffectNet in Section 4.4.4; Figure 2 is the RAFDB comparison. No curve values are stated in text. Training accuracy saturation does not establish zero error on completely random labels.
rows.check: Training-accuracy saturation does not establish perfect fit; its level is unavailable. Split the combined training/test measures and dataset-specific trajectories: Section 4.4.4 reports RAFDB, FERPlus and AffectNet-8, whereas the row condition names only RAFDB. DNFER is a comparator, not the baseline needed to establish perfect training fit. These aggregate trajectories also do not identify clean-label versus noisy-label learning order.
